summary.text: A woman was brought to hospital by her husband after five days of acute behavioural changes with paranoia, auditory hallucination, lack of sleep and labile mood, plus a week of headache, in the setting of recent exam and work stress. She had no psychiatric or illicit drug history. In the emergency department she was paranoid and confused with normal initial investigations apart from a mildly raised white cell count, and was referred to psychiatry for first-episode psychosis.

She then became febrile at 38.5°C with more confusion; lumbar puncture showed raised CSF protein and a mononuclear-predominant white cell count, and she was diagnosed with possible infective encephalitis and started on ceftriaxone and acyclovir with admission changed to medical. Brain MRI and CSF herpes and varicella PCR were negative or normal, yet her GCS fell to as low as five with catatonia despite antibiotics.

After one week, with neurology input, autoimmune and possible anti-NMDAR encephalitis was suspected and a pelvic ultrasound suggested a teratoma. She received intravenous immunoglobulin, methylprednisone and rituximab, had a laparotomy with right-side oophorectomy, and spent twenty days in ICU; her admission was complicated by a seizure, autonomic dysfunction and orofacial dyskinesia. EEG showed diffuse delta brush activity and CSF NMDAR antibody was positive, confirming anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

On discharge she needed ongoing cognitive rehabilitation and was transferred to a rehabilitation centre, where she progressed in behaviour and cognition, returned to her pre-morbid functional level and activities and has had no relapse in symptoms.
